item.title: Potato, tomahto: the roots of the modern tater
item.description:
A meet-cute millions of years ago gave rise to the tubers of today’s potatoes. A surprising potato–tomato tryst about nine million years ago might have led to the characteristic underground tuber of the modern potato (Solanum spp.)1.

References

item.title: Intricate origins of ice mummy’s ink revealed
item.description:
Imaging suggests that more than one tattooist applied pigment to the hands and forearms of a woman who lived more than two millennia ago. The Pazyryk people, who lived in the Altai Mountains of Siberia more than 2,000 years ago, are known for their intricate tattoos featuring animals in action. Now, a 3D scan of a mummy provides details of this body art, revealing for the first time some of the techniques used by these ancient tattooists1.

References

  1. Caspari, G., Deter-Wolf, A., Riday, D., Vavulin, M. & Pankova, S. Antiquity https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2025.10150 (2025).

item.title: Lava planets’ atmospheres give away what lies beneath
item.description:
Modelling suggests that data collected by JWST will be able to distinguish between planets that are molten to the core and those that are not. Far-off ‘lava worlds’ might hide something beneath their magma surface. Astronomers say we might be able to tell how molten a distant planet is by studying its surface temperature and the chemicals in its atmosphere1.

References

  1. Boukaré, C.-É. et al. Nature Astron. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-025-02617-4 (2025).

item.title: ‘Wind droughts’ driven by climate change put green power at risk
item.description:
Warming in the Arctic shifts storm patterns, leading to reductions in wind speeds in places that rely on turbines for clean electricity. One-fifth of the world’s wind turbines are in areas where winds could drop for long periods in the future1.

item.title: Unexpected danger lurks in this giant fault in the Yukon
item.description:
The Tintina fault has triggered many more earthquakes than was thought — and a build-up of strain poses a hazard. A giant geological fault in northwestern Canada threatens to unleash a huge earthquake in the historic gold-mining heart of the Yukon Territory1.

item.title: Rumble in the Miocene: terror bird versus caiman
item.description:
Toothmarks on a fossilized bone tell a story of two mega-predators. One day in the Middle Miocene epoch, some 11 million to 16 million years ago, a roughly 4.8-metre-long caiman ate a terror bird1.

item.title: Ageing stem cells in the knees drive arthritis damage
item.description:
Mice with a version of osteoarthritis experienced symptom relief after expression of a protein targeting a stem-cell receptor was blocked. A distinct population of stem cells helps to drive osteoarthritis, a degenerative joint disease that affects more than half a billion people worldwide1.

item.title: ‘Immortal’ stars have an elixir of youth: dark matter
item.description:
Modelling suggests that annihilation of this strange, invisible matter helps stars to retain that youthful glow. The Universe has an anti-ageing secret. Dark matter, the mysterious stuff that holds galaxies together, might also grant stars immortality, physicists say1.

item.title: Asia’s haze affects ice and weather on the Frozen Continent
item.description:
Pollution emitted by fossil-fuel usage in Asia influences sea-ice coverage in Antarctica. Tiny particles of pollution spewed into the atmosphere across Asia can affect climate as far away as Antarctica1.

item.title: How the world’s biggest bats got their enormous wingspans
item.description:
Genetic analysis helps to reveal why flying foxes can measure almost 2 metres from wingtip to wingtip. Island life has given the world’s largest bats their gargantuan wingspans, which can reach nearly 2 metres1.

item.title: How sugar overload in early life affects the brain later
item.description:
A study in mice finds that a high-sucrose diet during youth has long-term implications for learning and brain connectivity. A sugary diet in early life rewires the brains of mice, affecting their learning as adults1.

item.title: The mysterious missing ingredient in the highest-energy cosmic rays
item.description:
Data from a South Pole observatory show that the fraction of protons in ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays is lower than expected. The most energetic breed of particle ever observed might be more than meets the eye — or the particle detector. Physicists once thought that these rare particles, called ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays, encompassed only protons, but a study published today1 says otherwise.

item.title: Lonely spacecraft can navigate the stars
item.description:
NASA’s New Horizons probe, which hurtled past Pluto in 2015, demonstrates that it can sail through interstellar space using its onboard camera. NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft has ventured so far from the Sun that, in its view, nearby stars have moved substantially from their positions as seen from Earth. Researchers have now shown that the probe could use this effect for interstellar navigation, much like ships triangulate their position at sea using landmarks such as known lighthouses1.

  1. Lauer, T. R. et al. Astron. J. 170, 22 (2025).

item.title: Workouts can help gut microbes to quell cancer
item.description:
Mice that exercised produced higher levels of an immune-cell-stimulating molecule than sedentary rodents did. Exercise helps the immune system to fight tumours by stimulating microbes in the gut to make a compound known as formate, studies in mice have shown1.

item.title: Memory gets a boost from positive emotion
item.description:
Study participants’ memory faltered when they learnt while experiencing negative or neutral emotions. Objects are more memorable when people encounter them while feeling positive emotions than while feeling negative ones, according to an experimental study1 that offers insights into how emotions influence learning.

item.title: Hot air: the most extreme heatwaves are accelerating the fastest
item.description:
Tropical regions where heatwaves are already common will be hardest hit by this trend. The frequency of the longest and most dangerous heatwaves is increasing as the planet warms, research suggests1.

item.title: How breaking the ‘reciprocity law’ could improve green energy
item.description:
A material that emits less energy than it absorbs has the potential to save some of the sunlight wasted by solar collectors. Matter tends to emit thermal radiation at the same rate at which it absorbs it. But not all materials obey this ‘reciprocity’.

item.title: Poo of farm animals teems with drug-resistance genes
item.description:
A global map reveals the prevalence of thousands of genes that arm pathogens against antibiotics. An analysis of animal manure from 26 countries has identified global hotspots for antibiotic-resistance genes in livestock poo1.

item.title: Ancient DNA helps trace stinky Roman fish sauce to its source
item.description:
Mangled bones found at a one-time manufacturing facility pinpoint species used to make a quintessential condiment. Remnants of DNA extracted from bone fragments confirm that sardines were a major ingredient of the Roman Empire’s favourite fish sauce1.

item.title: Massive submarine eruption darkened clouds half a world away
item.description:
Sound-wave created by eruption in Tonga caused the atmosphere to warm over Mexico and the Caribbean. The 2022 eruption of a volcano in Tonga temporarily darkened clouds on the other side of the planet1.
